member.name: T:OpenIGI.Scripting.Expressions.ScriptExpressionEvaluator
member.summary: Evaluates a parsed expression, in whichever of the language's three types the caller asks for.

remarks.para: Transcribed from the original's three walks over the same tree — Expr_EvalInt (0x4B9120), Expr_EvalFloat (0x4B9660) and Expr_EvalString (0x4B8CE0). Which one runs is decided by the consumer, never by the expression: an assignment picks by its target's declared type, and a native picks per argument. The same source therefore has three different values depending on who asks, and this.vValue reading 0.75 as a float and 0 as an integer is correct behaviour rather than a rounding bug.
Behaviours that are observable and are reproduced deliberately rather than tidied:

item.description: Binary operands evaluate right-to-left in the integer walk, for every arithmetic, bitwise and comparison operator. With a call on each side — which retail menu scripts do have — the calls happen in that order, so this is not free to "correct". The float walk keeps that order except for -, which it alone evaluates left-first.
Division tests the divisor first and gives up before evaluating the numerator, in both numeric walks. f() / 0 never calls f.

An assignment evaluates its right-hand side twice. Expr_Assign evaluates it to store it, and then the caller evaluates the same node again to produce the assignment's own value — which is how the walks get a result in their type from a store made in the target's. So this.nUserData = Config_GetFlags() calls the native twice, and that is not a transcription slip.
The comma evaluates left first, then right, and yields the right. In the float walk it runs the integer evaluator on both sides.
Division by zero yields zero and raises the script error flag rather than faulting.
The float walk has no bitwise or shift operators at all — no case in the switch — so each one falls through to zero there.

remarks.para: Shifts take only the low byte of their right operand and >> is arithmetic, both straight from the original's use of a char shift count on a signed operand.

remarks.para: Behaviourally equivalent to Expr_Parse (0x4B9CD0) and its argument-list helper Expr_ParseArguments (0x4BA4C0). That is a deliberate divergence in method, not in result: with the same precedence and associativity rules — , transcribed verbatim — both produce the same tree, and the round trip is asserted in the tests.

Inside an argument list, , stops the expression instead of acting as the sequencing operator it is everywhere else. The original passes a flag that reclassifies the token.
), ;, { and } end an expression rather than being consumed by it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Scripting.Qvm.QvmOpcodeEncoding
member.summary: How a bytecode version numbers the opcodes.

remarks.para: is the meaning of an instruction and is numbered the way version 5 encodes it, because that is the version this port was written against. Version 7 gives the same instructions different numbers, so it needs a translation rather than a second opcode set: the language, the operand shapes and the interpreter are unchanged, and only the byte in the file moves.

Version 7 moves the control-flow group — RET through CALL, which version 5 puts at 0x13–0x18 — down to 0x02–0x07, and shifts everything from PUSH to POP up by six to fill the gap. BRK and NOP keep 0x00 and 0x01, and the whole arithmetic block from ADD at 0x19 to BLK at 0x2F is untouched, which is why a version 5 reader gets some way through a version 7 file before it desynchronises.

Read out of I.G.I. 2's own QVM_Open, which fills the 49-slot handler table one index at a time, and checked against every script in a retail installation: with this map a linear sweep lands exactly on the code-section boundary in all 1,784, which is what proves the operand widths.
